course.title: 24:7 Dad® A.M. (4th Edition)
course.description: Facilitation companion for the NFI 24:7 Dad® A.M. program — 12 weekly sessions built on the 5 Traits of the 24:7 Dad. Each session's agenda paces the class; present the licensed NFI slide deck via Zoom screen share and use the Fathering Handbook for take-home work. Slide numbers in each step refer to 24-7-Dad-AM_PPT.pptx. Program content © National Fatherhood Initiative; this companion contains structure and facilitator guidance only.

sessions.title: Session 1: The 5 Traits of the 24:7 Dad

steps.title: Welcome & program overview
steps.content:
## Welcome (slide 1)

- Welcome the group to the 24:7 Dad A.M. program — 12 weekly sessions.
- Introductions: name, children's names/ages, one hope for the program.
- Set group agreements (confidentiality, one voice at a time, phones down, honesty).
- Preview today's focus: the framework the whole program hangs on.

steps.title: The 5 Traits framework
steps.content:
Walk the trait wheel — the five areas the program builds:

1. **Self-Awareness**
2. **Caring for Self**
3. **Relationship Skills**
4. **Parenting Skills**
5. **Fathering Skills**

**Discussion:** which trait feels strongest for you today? Which one brought you here?

steps.title: Review questions
steps.content:
Run both review questions as **Vote activities** (Push an activity → Vote) so every dad answers on his own screen:

1. Naming the 5 traits (slide 4, options a–d).
2. How the 24:7 Dad uses self-awareness with his children (slide 5, options a–f).

After each vote closes, reveal the deck's answer on the slide and let the group react before moving on.

steps.title: Wrap-up & take-home
steps.content:
## Wrap-up

- Recap the session's key ideas in the group's own words.
- Point the group to the matching Fathering Handbook pages for Session 1.
- Ask each dad for one commitment to practice before the next session.
- Remind the group of the next session's date/time and thank them for showing up.

sessions.title: Session 2: What It Means to Be a Man

steps.content:
## Welcome back (slide 6)

- Check-in: how did last week's commitment go?
- Preview: where our ideas about "being a man" come from — and what they do to us.

steps.title: Cross-cultural traits of a man
steps.content:
## Traits of a man (slide 7)

The deck lists traits many cultures attach to manhood (self-confidence, courage, leadership, dependability, and also *controlling*).

**Discussion:** which of these did the men in your life model? Which serve you as a father, and which get in the way?

steps.title: Body image
steps.content:
## Body image (slide 8)

Culture sends unrealistic images of what men should look like.

**Discussion:** where do those messages show up (media, gym culture, childhood)? How do they land on our sons and daughters?

steps.title: Review questions
steps.content:
## Run the review

Run both review questions as **Vote activities** (Push an activity → Vote) so every dad answers on his own screen:

1. Whether today's culture links body image to being a man (slide 9, true/false).
2. Which source teaches most about what it means to be a man (slide 10, options a–e).

After each vote closes, reveal the deck's answer on the slide and let the group react before moving on.

steps.title: Showing and handling feelings
steps.content:
## Feelings (slide 12)

Key ideas from the deck: bottled-up feelings cause problems in body and mind; there are moments when holding a feeling is okay; what matters is *how* you show and handle them.

**Discussion:** what did your father do with his feelings? What do your children see you do?

steps.title: Grief and loss
steps.content:
## Grief and loss (slide 13)

Ungrieved losses follow us into health and relationships; crying is a primary human tool for grieving — and many boys are taught out of it.

**Discussion:** a loss you've carried (invite, don't require, sharing).

steps.title: Stress and anger
steps.content:
## Stress & anger (slides 17–18)

Mental and physical health feed each other; anger is energy — it's how the energy shows itself that causes trouble. Men often ignore warning signs until it's late.

**Discussion:** your body's early warning signs; what you do when the pressure spikes.

steps.title: Ways to communicate
steps.content:
## Communication styles (slide 22)

The 24:7 Dad owns his side of communication problems. Review the styles named in the deck (fight-or-flight, defensive/closed, good listener, open to change).

**Discussion:** which style is your default under stress?

steps.title: Talking with children
steps.content:
## Talking with children (slide 23)

Deck principles: honor what your children want, send good messages to yourself, avoid bad labels, focus on the goal and on what children learn.

**Practice:** pair up and rehearse one upcoming conversation with a child.

steps.title: The ideal father
steps.content:
## The ideal father (slide 27)

The ideal father has traits and duties tied to fathering *and* to his relationship with his children's mother.

**Discussion:** build the group's own 'ideal father' list on a whiteboard; compare with the deck.

steps.title: The benefits of marriage
steps.content:
## Benefits of marriage (slide 28)

The deck summarizes research on children raised by married parents across physical, social, mental, and financial health.

**Facilitator note:** handle with care for group members in other family structures — the point is what children need, not judgment.

steps.title: Morals and values
steps.content:
## Morals & values (slide 32)

'Discipline' comes from the Latin for *to teach, to guide*. Modeling is one of the most powerful ways parents transmit morals and values — on purpose and by accident.

**Discussion:** one value you want your children to carry, and how they currently see it in you.

steps.title: Discipline vs. punishment
steps.content:
## Discipline vs. punishment (slide 33)

Many fathers equate discipline with control and fear; punishment penalizes, discipline teaches. Rewards and freedoms work best used sparingly.

**Discussion:** how you were disciplined growing up vs. how you want to do it.

steps.title: Goals and self-worth
steps.content:
## Goals & self-worth (slide 37)

Children's self-worth rises when they meet the goals their father sets and falls when they can't. The skill: right-sized goals.

**Discussion:** a goal you hold for a child — is it theirs or yours, and is it within reach?

steps.title: Nature or nurture?
steps.content:
## Nature or nurture (slide 38)

Both shape who children become. Knowing your children's developmental milestones lets you support growth instead of fighting it.

**Activity:** match ages to milestones for the group's actual kids' ages.

steps.title: Ways to be involved
steps.content:
## Ways to be involved (slide 42)

Create a realistic plan for involvement in your children's lives — set yourself up for success rather than grand promises.

**Activity:** each dad drafts 2–3 concrete involvement actions for the next month.

steps.title: Helping children do well in school
steps.content:
## School success (slide 43)

The deck cites research: children with involved fathers get better grades and have fewer behavior problems — whether or not the father lives with them.

**Discussion:** one school-connected action available to you this month.

steps.title: Differences in beliefs and values
steps.content:
## Parenting differences (slide 47)

Differences in beliefs, morals, and values about parenting create real conflict. Solving a difference can mean changing or compromising — and getting change from the other parent starts with listening.

**Discussion:** one recurring difference and what it's really about.

steps.title: Her point of view
steps.content:
## Point of view (slide 48)

One of the hardest skills: seeing it from the other parent's side — and accepting she may never change hers.

**Practice:** state the mother's position on your recurring difference so fairly she'd agree with the summary.

steps.title: Work and family
steps.content:
## Work & family (slide 52)

Many fathers let work control their lives and shrink providing down to money alone.

**Discussion:** the ways a father provides beyond the paycheck — time, heart, mind, spirit.

steps.title: Balancing work and family
steps.content:
## Balance (slide 53)

Work–family conflict hurts children; balance isn't only more hours at home — it's *showing* you value both.

**Activity:** each dad names one visible signal of family-value he'll send this month.

steps.title: Program review: the 5 Traits
steps.content:
## The 5 Traits, revisited

Walk back through Self-Awareness, Caring for Self, Relationship Skills, Parenting Skills, and Fathering Skills.

**Discussion:** for each trait, one thing the group learned or changed.

steps.title: Reflections
steps.content:
## Reflections

Push a **Column feedback** activity (Push an activity → Column feedback) with columns like:

1. *What I'm taking with me*
2. *What I'm still working on*
3. *A word for the group*

Read the entries aloud as they come in.

steps.title: Graduation
steps.content:
## Graduation

- Present certificates one at a time; invite each dad to say a sentence about the father he's becoming.
- Share local follow-on resources and how to stay connected.
- Close the circle the way the group opened it in Session 1.
